title: Efficient Conversion of Carbon Dioxide on Atomically Dispersed Metal−Nx Species-Anchored Porous Carbon with Embedded CuxCoy Nanoparticles by Accelerating Electron Separation
abstract: To promote methanol product selectivity in CO2 reduction through photoelectrochemical reactions, a novel hybrid electrocatalyst (CuCo/NC) was developed to enhance electron transfer from cobalt to copper atoms with coordinated nitrogen on a ZIF-derived carbon matrix. The binding energies of Co 2p3/2 in CuCo/NC exhibited a 0.2 eV shifting to lower values, whereas those of Cu 2p3/2 exhibited a lower value shift by 1.5 eV, both of which contributed to electron transfer from Co to Cu. DFT calculations showed that the C−Co bond length (1.808 Å) between the CO* intermediate and CuCo/NC electrocatalyst was shorter than those in Cu/NC and Co/NC (1.946 and 1.870 Å, respectively), indicating that CO* was easier to adsorb on the CuCo/NC electrocatalyst for further reduction. The CuCo/NC electrocatalyst with stable properties efficiently converted CO2 into methanol (FE > 60%) with a carbon atom conversion rate of 4098 nmol h−1 cm−2.

KEYWORDS: CuCo alloy, Metal−Nx, CO2 photoelectrochemical reduction, DFT calculation, N-doped carbon material, EXAFS analysis
■ INTRODUCTION The electroreduction of CO2 into high-energy chemicals provides a potential strategy to achieve carbon-neutral energy circulation,1−3 while the energy supply is entirely dependent on electricity. An alternative way for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is utilizing renewable energy such as solar energy to reduce energy consumption.4 But the CO2 photocatalysis (PC) conversion generally yields a low efficiency of less than 2.0%.5 A solar photoelectrochemical (PEC) cell, which is composed of a photoanode and an electrocathode and can use solar energy and improve efficiency simultaneously, has recently attracted more attention. Among the available transformation approaches, converting CO2 into hydrocarbons with a high energy density is a promising strategy for utilizing CO2 resources.6,7 It is known that CO2RR to alcohols requires high energy barriers and proton coupling, which are multielectron steps, resulting in major challenges for low current density, poor selectivity, and large overpotential for the CO2 reaction.8,9 Thus, the development of highly active and robust electrocatalysts for CO2RR is required. Cu-based catalysts are the best metal catalysts capable of producing hydrocarbons, especially alcohol, for CO2RR, yet they have inherent drawbacks such as slow activities and selectivity.10−13 In order to more efficiently obtain hydrocarbon products, metal alloys or bimetallic catalysts have been proposed for CO2RR, acting through a lowering of the binding
energy required for intermediates of CO2RR and improving their inherent activity.14−16 For example, bimetallic Au/Cu was employed as a catalyst for the electrochemical synthesis of C2+ alcohols.17 Although the overpotential was only 265 mV, poor current efficiencies and partial current densities of alcohols caused a low CO2 reduction rate. Similarly, Sn/Cu bimetallic catalysts revealed excellent activity with a formic acid selectivity of 90.2%, while lacking multielectron products such as methanol and ethanol.18 Nevertheless, achieving a high selectivity and CO2 reduction rate simultaneously for CO2RR remains a challenge. Heteroatom-doped carbons, especially the catalytic nanocarbon materials decorated with active metal−Nx sites, have shown great potential in tackling the above challenges in CO2RR due to their abundant exposed atomic interfaces and fast electron transfer capacity.19,20 However, little progress has been made with regard to hydrocarbon production because the low metal content leads to a relatively large distance between

metal atoms, thus making it impossible to achieve further reduction of intermediate products. Subsequently, various studies have tried to combine bimetallic nanoparticles with heteroatom-doped carbon composites for CO2RR, for example, CuxNiy alloy nanoparticles embedded in a nitrogen−carbon network.21 Although the as-synthesized catalyst effectively converted CO2 into CO with a maximum Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 94.5%, it still lacked hydrocarbons due to the reduced binding energy of CO*. Pure Cu and Co catalysts have various inherent deficiencies in CO2RR catalysis. For example, Cu catalysts usually produce multiple products and thus lead to poor selectivity;22 this limitation generally arises from the moderate binding energy for most reaction intermediates. Similarly, Co-embedded nitrogen-rich carbon complexes tend to favor the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction in aqueous electrolytes.23
Herein, we developed a novel hybrid electrocatalyst for CO2RR composed of atomically dispersed metal−Nx species anchored onto a porous carbon (NC) matrix with embedded CuCo bimetallic nanoparticles, denoted as CuCo/NC. The assynthesized catalyst was able to effectively convert CO2 into alcohols, and in particular, methanol, overcoming the deficiencies of pure Cu and Co catalysts for CO2RR. Moreover, the CuCo/NC catalyst exhibited excellent stability during long-term electrolysis due to stabilization of the porous carbon matrix.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Materials. Analytical grade zinc nitrate hexahydrate, cobalt(II) chloride hexahydrate, copper nitrate hexahydrate, and 2-methyl imidazole were purchased from Sigma−Aldrich. Anhydrous n-hexane and anhydrous methanol were acquired from Shanghai Chemical Reagents, China. All the chemicals were used without any treatment. Copper foam (90 mesh, Betty New Energy Materials, China), titanium foil (99.7%, Baoji Titanium Co., Ltd., China), and Nafion membrane solution (5%, Shanghai Hesen Co. China) were used as materials for electrode preparation. Preparation of Electrodes. TiO2 Nanotube Anode. In a typical procedure, titanium foil was anodized at 45 V for 2.5 h with a mixed electrolyte (97.7% (CH2OH)2 + 2 vol % H2O + 0.3 wt % NH2F). The sample was then washed with ethanol and dried in the air. Finally, the amorphous TiO2 phase was calcinated at 450 °C in a muffle furnace for 3 h to form the stable anatase phase.24
CuCo/NC Cathode. Synthesis of ZIF-8. Typically, (1) 2.232 g of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O and (2) 2.464 g of 2-methylimidazole were dissolved in 60 mL of methanol separately. Subsequently, solution (1) was poured into solution (2) for ultrasonic treatment (15 min). The ZIF-8 sample was then grown under static conditions at 25 °C for 24 h. Products were obtained by centrifuging at ,000 rpm and drying in a vacuum at 60 °C for 12 h. Synthesis of CuCo/NC. Typically, ZIF-8 (200 mg) was poured in n-hexane (40 mL) for a bath sonication for 15 min. After forming a homogeneous solution, a Cu(NO3)2 aqueous solution(100 mg/mL, 250 μL) and a Co(NO3)2 aqueous solution (100 mg/mL, 250 μL) were added into the ZIF-8 solution drop by drop lasting 1 h under stirring. Next, the mixture continued to be stirred for 3 h at 25 °C to ensure that metal irons were fully absorbed onto the ZIF-8 framework. The resultant solid powders were collected by centrifuging several times and drying for 12 h (60 °C, vacuum). Subsequently, the dried solid powders were calcined at 900 °C for 2 h (heating rate 10 °C/min) in a pure nitrogen atmosphere at the rate of 100 sccm, leading to black-colored powder electrocatalysts (CuCo/ NC). Co/NC and Cu/NC samples were synthesized in the same way as CuCo/NC except for the lack of Cu(NO3)2 or Co(NO3)2. CuCo/NC@CF Cathode. Copper foam (CF, 1 cm × 1 cm) was used for the substrate. Briefly, the cathode catalysts (10 mg) were dispersed in a mixed solution (200 μL of Nafion solution + 1 mL of
deionized water) under ultrasonic treatment. The mixture was coated on the surface of CF dropwise and then dried in a vacuum at 80 °C overnight.
Characterization. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the catalysts were recorded on an X’Pert PRO diffractometer (PANanalytical, Netherlands) with Cu Kα radiation. High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images were obtained using a JEM-2100 (Japan) transmission electron microscope operating at 200 kV. The morphology of the catalysts was analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Hitachi SU-70 microscope, Japan). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed on a scanning Xray microprobe (PHI 5000 Verasa, ULAC-PHI, Inc.) using Al Ka radiation and the C 1s peak at 284.6 eV as the internal standard. Elemental analyses of Cu and Co in the catalysts were performed by inductively coupled plasma spectrometry (ICP-OES; PerkinElmer optima 8300). Adsorption−desorption isotherms were obtained to assess the pore parameters, including Brunauer−Emmett−Teller (BET) specific surface area and pore size. These were all performed on a Micromeritics Tristar II3020M. CO2 adsorption isotherms were obtained on an iSorb HP2 instrument (Quanta chrome Instruments). The samples were degassed at 0.001 Torr and 300 °C for 5 h before the measurements. Extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) measurements were collected on a BL14W1 station in Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The electron storage ring was operated at 3.5 GeV with a maximum current of 250 mA. Cu and Co K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) data were recorded in a fluorescence mode. Cu and Co foils were used as references.
Photoelectrochemical Reduction of CO2. The CO2 photoelectrochemical reduction reaction was detected in a sealed H-cell separated by a Nafion membrane. The cathode chamber and the anode chamber were poured into 20 mL of 0.5 M H2SO4 and NaHCO3 solutions, respectively. A xenon lamp (SOLAREDGE700, 300W, 10 mW cm−2) was used as simulated sunlight. All electrocatalytic activity tests were detected on an electrochemical workstation (Ivium, Netherlands). CO2 was continuously purged into the cathodic compartment (25 mL min−1) through a gas diffuser during the constant potential electrolysis.
The gaseous product was collected by a reservoir bag and analyzed using gas chromatography (GC7820A, Agilent). The liquid products were composed of acids and alcohols. The former was detected on an ion chromatograph (ICS 2000, Dionex, IonPac AS11-HC analytical column Φ4 × 250 mm), and the latter was detected by gas chromatography (GC 6890 N, Agilent, DB-624 column Φ30 m × 0.53 mm × 3 μm).
Calculation Method and Modeling. The Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP) code was used to carry out the DFT calculations for the catalysts. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) within the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) form was used as the exchange−correlation function. The model for the Cu/NC sample was modeled by anchoring a Cu nanoparticle in Cu−N4 decorated graphene, which was based on the EXAFS fitting analysis. The model for Co/NC was similar to that of Cu/NC. As for CuCo/ NC, it was demonstrated that the composition of CuCo/NC was complicated, including Cu nanoparticles, Co nanoparticles, and CuCo alloy nanoparticles. Furthermore, there also existed Cu−N, Co−N, and Cu−Co−N sites. To show the difference among the samples, as well as to simplify the calculation, here we just used a CuCo nanoparticle doped on the substrate. The distance between the metal NPs was not considered in this Article. According to the previous study, here we used the metal cluster with 12 atoms, and the number of Co was 4 on the basis of ICP mass spectrometry.25 In the same way, there existed Cu−N4, Co−N4, and Cu−Co coordination in CuCo/NC indicated by EXAFS curves, so we chose a possible structure (Cu−Co−N6) to simplify the calculation. The vacuum layer and the kinetic-energy cutoff of the plane-wave expansion were set to 20 Å and 600 eV, respectively. The Brillouin zone was sampled with a

B
3 × 3 × 1 k-mesh in the Monkhorst−Park scheme. The forces on each atom were optimized to be less than 0.05 eV A−1.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The morphology of CuCo/NC was shown in Figure 1a and b. CuCo/NC had a three-dimensional structure, embedded with nanoparticles with an average diameter of 11.4 nm. For comparison, Cu/NC (Figure S1a) and Co/NC(Figure S1e) catalysts had a similar morphology, with average nanoparticle diameters of 14.3 and 12.9 nm, respectively. HRTEM (Figure 1c) confirmed that the Cu/Co bimetallic alloy was encapsulated in a carbon shell, with lattice spacings of 0.34 and 0.21 nm, corresponding to the (002) plane of graphitic carbon and the (111) plane of the Cu/Co bimetallic alloy,26
respectively. Correspondingly, XRD patterns (Figure 1 g) of all three samples exhibited peaks between 20°and 30°, which were assigned to the (002) plane of graphitic carbon. The remaining peaks observed in Cu/NC and Co/NC were part of Cu (PDF 65-9026) and Co (PDF 15-0806). A new broad peak at 43.9°, lying between the 44.2° peak for Co(111) and the 43.3° peak for Cu(111), was observed in the CuCo/NC sample, implying the insertion of more Co atoms into the Cu lattice to form bimetallic CuCo(111).27 The corresponding energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) element mapping (Figure 1d) showed that copper and cobalt agglomerated into particles partly. Additionally, the aberration-corrected high resolution
HAADF-STEM image (Figure 1e) exhibited many bright spots, which indicated the formation of metal−Nx bonding. Also, Figure 1f showed many neighboring dual-dots. These neighboring dual-dots suggested the formation of diatomic sites. The above results confirmed the coexistence of Cu and Co single atoms and CuCo nanoparticles across the entire carbon matrix of CuCo/NC. A similar distribution was observed for Cu/NC (Figure S1b−d) and Co/NC (Figure S 1f−h). CuCo/NC had nearly 4.0 wt % Cu and 1.6 wt % Co, as determined by ICP mass spectrometry, compared with Cu/NC (5.6 wt %) and Co/NC (3.2 wt %). Figure S2a showed N2 adsorption−desorption for Cu/NC, Co/NC, and CuCo/NC catalysts. The BET surface areas of the Cu/NC, Co/NC, and CuCo/NC samples were 784.1, 604.5, and 793.7 m2 g−1, respectively. Moreover, Figure S2b showed an average diameter of mesopores of approximately 4 nm for all samples. The large specific surface area increased the adsorption site of CO2 and intermediates, thus further enhancing the mass transfer and the rate of reaction. The chemical composition and elemental states of the
samples were investigated by XPS. The high-resolution Cu 2p3/2 spectrum(Figure 2b) exhibited two deconvoluted peaks at 932.7 and 934.9 eV, assigned to Cu0(possibly existing as Cu+) and Cu2+-N/C species, respectively.28 The Auger Cu LMM spectrum exhibited a peak at 570.2 eV (Figure S3), demonstrating the presence of Cu+ species.29 XPS confirmed
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00652 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
that both Cu/NC and CuCo/NC catalysts existed Cu nanoparticles and Cu−N species. Metallic Co, Co−O, and Co−N/C peaks, located at 779.7, 780.8, and 782.2 eV respectively, were observed from the Co 2p3/2 spectra of both Co/NC and CuCo/NC (Figure 2a).30,31 Owing to the similar binding energies between the Co−N and Co−C bonds, the peak at 782.2 eV could be assigned to either Co−N or Co−C, thus there exists a heterostructure between Co and carbon in Co/NC and CuCo/NC. The carbon shell covering the surface of Co nanoparticles can prevent Co nanoparticles from accumulating during CO2RR, further improving the electrochemical performance of the catalysts. The formation of Co−O bond was due to the oxidation of Co on the surface. Furthermore, it was found that the Co 2p binding energies of CuCo/NC(Figure 2a) exhibited a 0.2 eV shift to lower values compared with those of Co/NC, indicating Co in CuCo/NC possessed a higher valence state than that of Co/NC. Additionally, the binding energy of Cu 2p3/2 in Cu/NC (Figure 2b) was 1.5 eV higher than that of CuCo/NC, revealing that a part of electron of Co given to adjacent Cu.21
The high resolution N 1s spectra of all the samples evidenced the presence of pyridinic N (398.9 eV), Cu/Co−N (399.5 eV), pyrrolic N (400.9 eV), and graphitic N (402.1 eV) species.32 Compared with Co/NC (8.23 atom %) and Cu/NC (7.60 atom %), the N content of CuCo/NC (9.65 atom %) was much higher than those of Cu/NC and Co/NC (Figure 2c,d), indicating an enhanced N doping efficiency for CuCo/ NC. Pyridinic N and pyrrolic N, as active sites for CO2RR, 33
accounted for 73% of the total N content in CuCo/NC, higher than in Co/NC (59.7%) and Cu/NC (54.1%). Furthermore, the presence of Cu/Co−N species in all samples indicated the existence of metal−N bonds other than nanoparticles. To further assess the electronic structures and local
coordination environment of the Cu and Co species, XANES and EXAFS analyses were performed. The position of the absorption edge for CuCo/NC and Cu/NC was between the Cu foil and CuO (Figure 3a), indicating that Cu0 and Cu−N− C coexist in both CuCo/NC and Cu/NC samples. The XANES spectra at the Co K-edge of Co/NC and CuCo/NC were observed to be similar to the Cu K-edge (Figure 3c). The absorption edges of the two samples were located between those for Co and CoO, likely due to the coordination of Co− N/C. Furthermore, the valence state of the Cu atoms in CuCo/NC was slightly lower than that in Cu/NC, while the valence state of Co in CuCo/NC was significantly higher than that in Co/NC. Thus, it is likely that electron transfer from Co to Cu atoms occurred, leading to Cu bonding with Co in CuCo/NC. The EXAFS curves for CuCo/NC and Cu/NC showed a dominant metallic Cu−Cu coordination with a peak at 2.2 Å (Figure 3b). The peak at 1.5 Å corresponded to the Cu−N/C scattering pair, which further demonstrated the existence of Cu−N4 coordination in CuCo/NC and Cu/Cu− N−C samples.34,35 The EXAFS spectra in R-space and K-space (Figure 3d and e and Table S1) for CuCo/NC were different from those of Co/NC, indicating that the coordination environments of Co in CuCo/NC were different from those
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00652 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
in Co/NC. Two peaks at 1.4 and 2.2 Å, for CuCo/NC and Co/Co−N−C, were ascribed to the Co−N4 and Co−Co coordinations, respectively.36,37 Moreover, the peak at 2.9 Å, for CuCo/NC, was attributed to Cu−Co coordination. Furthermore, the Cu−Cu bond length in CuCo/NC shifted to 2.207 Å, shorter than the Cu−Cu bond length in the Cu foil (2.240 Å), while the length of the Co−Co bond in CuCo/NC was 2.203 Å, larger than that in the Co foil (2.171 Å). The above result demonstrated the existence of the Cu−Co bond in CuCo/NC again. The wavelet transform contour plots of CuCo/NC (Figure 3f) exhibited the Co−N, Co−Co, and Co− Cu bonds, once again showing the existence of Co−Cu coordination. The electrocatalytic activity of CuCo/NC, Cu/NC, and Co/
NC on CO2RR was assessed using a two-compartment cell
with a 0.5 M CO2-saturated NaHCO3 electrolyte. As shown in Figure 4a, CuCo/NC exhibited the highest total current density from −0.4 V to −1.4 V (vs RHE), giving current densities of 15.5 mA cm−2 at −1.3 V (vs RHE), significantly exceeding those of Cu/NC and Co/NC. When tested in a N2saturated NaHCO3 solution, we can find a much smaller current density compared with that in a CO2-saturated NaHCO3 solution, showing that CuCo/NC was much more efficient for CO2RR. Current−time experiments of the photoelectric cell were performed with different conditions and are shown in Figure S4c. The current density was much higher under light conditions than that of under dark conditions, demonstrating that the anode under light conditions vastly promoted CO2RR.
38 The experiments for the photoelectrochemical CO2 reduction reaction were
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00652 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
detected in a photoelectric cell. The gaseous and liquid products formed in the CO2 reduction were analyzed by gas chromatography and ion chromatography. The FE of the products generated from three catalysts at −2 V (Figure 4b) showed that, in a 0.5 M NaHCO3 electrolyte, N−C had the poorest CO2RR activity, which possessed the maximum FEH2 (80.1%) as well as the lowest current density. This indicated that the nonmetallic N-doped catalyst had poor selectivity and activity for CO2RR. Correspondingly, Cu/NC and Co/NC showed similar results that H2 was also the major part of the product for CO2RR. Conversely, CuCo/NC reached a maximum methanol FE of 60.2%, 2.9 and 2.4 times higher than Cu/NC and Co/NC, respectively. Such a high FE(CH3OH) of CuCo/NC provided a maximum carbon atom conversion rate of 4098 nmol h−1 cm−2, approximately 1.9 times and 1.7 times those of Co/NC (2144 nmol h−1 cm−2) and Cu/NC (2360 nmol h−1 cm−2), respectively(Figure 4c). As shown in Table S3, CuCo/NC reached a much higher FE of CH3OH production than those of other Cu-based catalysts. The above results showed that the combination of the high content of CuCo alloy and unsaturated metal−Nx sites can accelerate the reaction rate for CO2 reduction. Additionally, the catalytic performance of CuCo/NC was highly stable, showing n undiminished current density after 7 h in the CO2-saturated NaHCO3 solution (Figure S4b). HRTEM of CuCo/NC following the stability test (Figure S4a) showed no apparent changes in morphology, demonstrating the excellent stability of CuCo/NC under CO2RR conditions.
To further explore the origin of excellent activity of the CuCo/NC catalyst, electrochemically active surface areas were detected for the catalysts which is shown in Figure S5.39 The double-layer capacitance of CuCo/NC (5.17 mF cm−2) was approximately twice that of Cu/NC (2.97 mF cm−2) and Co/ NC (3.67 mF cm−2). The large electrochemically active surface area provided a large amount of active sites, thus enhancing the performance of CuCo/NC for CO2RR. The reaction kinetics of different catalysts for CO2RR were further explored as below. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy results showed a smaller semicircular diameter of CuCo/NC compared with the Co/NC and Cu/NC samples (Figure S4d), implying a lower charge transfer resistance of CuCo/NC and therefore a faster electron transfer to CO2 to generate various intermediates. Thus, CuCo/NC led to an immensely enhanced catalytic efficiency for CO2 reduction. 40
Moreover, it is well-known that 3D porous N-doped carbon materials have a great CO2 adsorption capacity,
41,42 contributing to the enhancement of activity observed herein. To verify this, CO2 adsorption isotherms of the three samples were obtained (Figure 4d). The CO2 adsorption capacity of the CuCo/NC catalyst reached 3.42 mmol g−1, much higher than those of Co/NC (2.12 mmol g−1) and Cu/NC (2.59 mmol g−1). Thus, the large CO2 adsorption capacity of the CuCo/NC catalyst facilitated the adsorption of considerable amounts of CO2 on its surface, thus promoting its catalytic performance.
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00652 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
In order to theoretically assess the CO2RR activity of CuCo/ NC, DFT calculations of different catalysts were performed as below. Compared with the other two catalysts (Co/NC and Cu/NC), the calculated Bader charges of CuCo/NC (Table S2) showed that the Cu atoms and Co atoms were +0.07 and +0.26, respectively, revealing the electron transfer from Co to Cu (in agreement with the XANES analysis). The formed intermediate (COOH*) on the surface of CuCo/NC exhibited the lowest free energy, indicating that COOH* was more stable than others, which was likely due to the greater negative charge of the Cu atoms (Figure 5a). The COOH* species were further reduced to the CO* intermediate.43 On the basis ofthe Brønsted−Evans−Polanyi relationship,44 the reaction barrier had a linear relationship to the reaction energy; thus, the step involving the COOH* reduction to CO* was a ratelimiting step for all the samples here. Compared with Co/NC and Cu/NC catalysts, the free energy of CO* over the CuCo/ NC catalyst was more negative, likely due to the more active Cu atoms. Furthermore, the minimum C−M bond (Figure 5b)
between CuCo/NC−CO* was 1.808 Å, shorter than those of Cu/NC−CO* (1.946 Å) and Co/NC−CO* (1.870 Å). The bond lengths of C−O were 1.190 Å (CuCo/NC), 1.191 Å (Cu/NC), and 1.196 Å (Co/NC), revealing that the CO* adsorbed on CuCo/NC was much more stable than others. The above results indicated that it was easier for CO* to adsorb onto the CuCo/NC catalyst surface to be further reduced to the CHO* intermediate, thus further accelerating the formation of methanol product. In conclusion, CuCo/NC was efficient and stable for the CO2 reduction reaction, especially for methanol formation. The enhanced electrocatalytic activity of CuCo/NC was because of stabilized COOH* and CO* adsorption on the surface of the CuCo/NC catalyst. On the basis of the above results of DFT calculations, a
possible pathway for CO2RR on CuCo/NC was proposed as shown in Figure 5c. In the initial stage of reduction, CO2 adsorbs onto the catalyst surface to transfer into CO2
•−.45 The adsorbed CO2 •− then binds to Cu atoms of the CuCo/NC
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c00652 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
G
sample and accelerates the conversion for COOH* to CO* intemediates, which was important for methanol formation.22 The abundant active sites on the surface of CuCo/NC further accelerate the CO* species to be reduced to CHO*, eventually resulting in CH3OH formation. The high electrocatalytic activity of CuCo/NC was on account of the following reasons: First, the 3D macroporous structure with a coordinated N component allows numerous effective catalyst sites to interact with CO2, facilitating CO2 retention for further reduction. Moreover, the enhanced electron transfer from Co to Cu atoms leads to the more stable adsorption structure to hold COOH* and CO*, allowing the conversion of CO* to methanol, as verified by DFT calculations. All in all, both the 3D porous coordinated N species-anchored carbon structure and the CuCo alloy are crucial for methanol formation.
■ CONCLUSION Herein, we have prepared a CuCo/NC catalyst with CuCo alloy nanoparticles embedded in a highly porous coordinated N species-anchored carbon matrix able to synergistically catalyze CO2 to methanol. The highly porous coordinated N species anchored-carbon matrix improves the CO2 adsorption as well as stabilizes CuCo nanoparticles during long-term electrolysis. Further, the enhanced electron transfer from Co to Cu atoms leads to the more stable adsorption structure to hold COOH* and CO*, allowing the conversion of CO* to methanol. The CuCo/NC catalyst exhibits a maximum FE of 60.2% toward methanol and an excellent carbon atom conversion rate of 4098 nmol h−1 cm−2 with stable properties. The present work opens up enormous possibilities for the rational design of metal electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction under mild conditions, especially for metals with a low intrinsic activity.
